references_named: Walter Benjamin, 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' (1935)
rationale: Provenance turns the browser's history.length and document.referrer into a museum-style chain-of-custody panel that the privacy web makes structurally unreadable — the redaction bars are not a graphic effect but the honest shape of what the browser will disclose, and the 'Transfer to a new owner' button uses history.pushState to extend the ledger without navigation or network. Concept and execution collapse (P1): the mechanism of redacted chain-of-custody IS the provenance argument, and the witty surface (a comically empty museum plate) carries a precise art-historical point about Haacke's owner-by-owner demystification and Benjamin's aura-as-history, punctured by the privacy stance that proves the critic's point for them (P6/P7/P8). Voice is dry, intelligent, cheerful-cynic; restraint is strong; the build is the minimum necessary.
reservations: The leverage of privacy-engineering blackouts is the work's load-bearing claim and works only because referrer/referrer-policy has become aggressive by default; older browsers or Referrer-Policy: unsafe-url origins would leak the prior owner and collapse the artwork's premise into legible text. Conceptually rigorous but mechanically conditional in a way the page itself does not flag.
revision_suggestion: Add a one-line note or visual that attests the conditional privacy posture (e.g., when the referrer IS disclosed, the prior-owner's origin is rendered as text rather than a redaction bar), so the work's claim — 'the privacy web redacts everything' — stays legible regardless of browser, and turns the conditional into part of the piece rather than a quiet failure mode.
